title: 1. Ask your protagonist about their hopes and dreams—and really listen.
use_cases: Use when defining a protagonist's internal motivations beyond the immediate plot
Implement when aligning a character's personal dreams with the central conflict
Configure when troubleshooting a character who lacks agency or initiative
content:
![](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEhxtazy-vE5JIjKTSVVHiTlXtJUgXSJdQcTZS3o83fhk6MYySruGr-615lZwsOOWID1bOJwfJklCkS-iH5hHuwiqZ5dLqMl4brIscXeGiHjCDkSt8GzKjWPqQfVRTSAG2IwrEg_i3wKfyfT/w183-h200/0456a735b30afb7b67d84563484b99ab.jpg)

Look at the character’s goals and determine what they want as a person, not the character you created to fill the role of protagonist. Is it only what the plot says they ought to go after, or is there more? Give them goals and desires that align with what the plot also needs. For example, in the movie Stargate, Danial Jackson is an archaeologist with a crazy theory that someone other than the Egyptians built the pyramids. His peers think he’s nuts, but he’s sure he’s right, and he dreams of proving his theories one day. This dream gives him the agency he needs when offered a chance to translate ancient hieroglyphs that will ultimately prove he was right. He doesn’t know that at first, but the offer coincides with his dreams.(Here’s more on Beware the Vague Goal When Outlining a Scene)
